items.stem: Which city adopted Kate Raworth's "doughnut" model as a basis for policy in 2020?
items.answer: Amsterdam
items.markingKey: Amsterdam. The model sets a social foundation and an ecological ceiling.

items.stem: Explain why a circular economy can increase resource security.
items.answer: Keeping materials in use through reuse, repair, remanufacturing and recycling reduces demand for virgin resources and imports, cuts waste and emissions, and protects supply of critical materials.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Keeping materials in use through reuse, repair, remanufacturing and recycling reduces demand for virgin resources and imports, cuts waste and emissions, and protects supply of critical materials. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Banning plastic bags solves the plastic pollution problem." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Bags are a small share of plastic waste; bans must be combined with wider reductions, deposit schemes and better waste management.
items.markingKey: Bags are a small share of plastic waste; bans must be combined with wider reductions, deposit schemes and better waste management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A data table shows the daily water use per person in a city in California: 1990 - 212.0 litres; 2010 - 144.3 litres. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (144.3 − 212.0) ÷ 212.0 × 100; A1 -31.9% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Australia: ecological footprint ≈ 6.4 gha/person; biocapacity ≈ 12.3 gha/person. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Calculate (a) the ecological balance per person and (b) how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average resident.
items.answer: (a) +5.9 gha per person (ecological reserve) (b) 6.4 / 1.6 ≈ 4.0 Earths
items.markingKey: (a) M1 biocapacity − footprint, A1 +5.9 gha and correct label. (b) M1 A1 4.0 Earths.

items.stem: Define the term "linear economy".
items.answer: The "take-make-dispose" model in which raw materials are extracted, made into products and discarded
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the "take-make-dispose" model in which raw materials are extracted, made into products and discarded. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a circular economy and a linear economy.
items.answer: A linear economy follows take-make-dispose; a circular economy keeps materials in loops through reuse, repair and recycling, designing out waste.
items.markingKey: A linear economy follows take-make-dispose; a circular economy keeps materials in loops through reuse, repair and recycling, designing out waste. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a circular economy and a linear economy.
items.answer: A linear economy follows take-make-dispose; a circular economy keeps materials in loops through reuse, repair and recycling, designing out waste.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Circular economy policies are only relevant to rich countries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Repair, reuse and informal recycling are widespread in low-income countries (e.g. Dharavi in Mumbai), and circular models can create jobs.
items.markingKey: Repair, reuse and informal recycling are widespread in low-income countries (e.g. Dharavi in Mumbai), and circular models can create jobs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using informal recycling in Dharavi, Mumbai as an example, explain the informal circular economy.
items.answer: Thousands of small units recycle plastics, metals and paper, employing many thousands of people. Informal workers recover materials efficiently but face health and safety risks.
items.markingKey: Context (Thousands of small units recycle plastics, metals and paper, employing many thousands of people.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Informal workers recover materials efficiently but face health and safety risks. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the informal circular economy.

items.stem: Suggest two ways that a school could apply the circular economy.
items.answer: A uniform and textbook reuse scheme; composting canteen waste; buying refillable and repairable equipment; recycling e-waste.
items.markingKey: A uniform and textbook reuse scheme; composting canteen waste; buying refillable and repairable equipment; recycling e-waste.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "payments for ecosystem services"?
options: Management of local resources such as forests, water or wildlife by the communities that depend on them
An economic system that designs out waste, keeps products and materials in use and regenerates natural systems, in contrast to "take-make-dispose"
The careful and responsible management of resources to ensure they are available for future generations
Schemes that pay landowners to manage land to provide services such as forest carbon storage or clean water, e.g. Costa Rica's PSA programme
items.answer: Schemes that pay landowners to manage land to provide services such as forest carbon storage or clean water, e.g. Costa Rica's PSA programme
items.markingKey: D. "payments for ecosystem services" is schemes that pay landowners to manage land to provide services such as forest carbon storage or clean water, e.g. Costa Rica's PSA programme.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "resource stewardship"?
options: The eight international development goals for 2000-2015, such as halving extreme poverty
Schemes that pay landowners to manage land to provide services such as forest carbon storage or clean water, e.g. Costa Rica's PSA programme
A view that human ingenuity and technology will overcome resource limits, as argued by Julian Simon
The careful and responsible management of resources to ensure they are available for future generations
items.answer: The careful and responsible management of resources to ensure they are available for future generations
items.markingKey: D. "resource stewardship" is the careful and responsible management of resources to ensure they are available for future generations.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "doughnut economics"?
options: The eight international development goals for 2000-2015, such as halving extreme poverty
Kate Raworth's model of a safe and just space between a social foundation of human needs and an ecological ceiling of planetary boundaries
A view that human ingenuity and technology will overcome resource limits, as argued by Julian Simon
The careful and responsible management of resources to ensure they are available for future generations
items.answer: Kate Raworth's model of a safe and just space between a social foundation of human needs and an ecological ceiling of planetary boundaries
items.markingKey: B. "doughnut economics" is Kate Raworth's model of a safe and just space between a social foundation of human needs and an ecological ceiling of planetary boundaries.

items.stem: Leila writes: "The SDGs are legally binding treaties." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They are a non-binding political commitment; countries report progress voluntarily.
items.markingKey: They are a non-binding political commitment; countries report progress voluntarily. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Banning plastic bags solves the plastic pollution problem." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Bags are a small share of plastic waste; bans must be combined with wider reductions, deposit schemes and better waste management.
items.markingKey: Bags are a small share of plastic waste; bans must be combined with wider reductions, deposit schemes and better waste management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between cornucopian views and neo-Malthusian views.
items.answer: Neo-Malthusians argue population and consumption growth will exceed environmental limits; cornucopians argue technology, markets and innovation will expand resources.
items.markingKey: Neo-Malthusians argue population and consumption growth will exceed environmental limits; cornucopians argue technology, markets and innovation will expand resources. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between bottom-up resource management and top-down resource management.
items.answer: Top-down management is directed by governments or international bodies; bottom-up management is led by local communities and users.
items.markingKey: Top-down management is directed by governments or international bodies; bottom-up management is led by local communities and users. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why recycling rates vary between countries.
items.answer: They depend on infrastructure (collection, sorting, processing), policy (landfill taxes, deposit schemes, extended producer responsibility), markets for recycled materials and public attitudes - Germany recycles about two-thirds of municipal waste, many low-income countries very little.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They depend on infrastructure (collection, sorting, processing), policy (landfill taxes, deposit schemes, extended producer responsibility), markets for recycled materials and public attitudes - Germany recycles about two-thirds of municipal waste, many low-income countries very little. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Planetary boundaries are fixed thresholds that cause immediate collapse when crossed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They mark zones of increasing risk based on uncertain science; crossing them raises the likelihood of abrupt, irreversible change.
items.markingKey: They mark zones of increasing risk based on uncertain science; crossing them raises the likelihood of abrupt, irreversible change. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

The following information is provided.

Graph description: Costa Rica forest cover (% of land area) - 1940: 75; 1987: 21; 2000: 47; 2021: 57.

Explain how policy contributed to the change after 1987.
items.answer: A 1996 Forest Law banned conversion of forest; Payments for Environmental Services (1997) rewarded conservation and reforestation; ecotourism created income from standing forest.
items.markingKey: A 1996 Forest Law banned conversion of forest; Payments for Environmental Services (1997) rewarded conservation and reforestation; ecotourism created income from standing forest. items.stem: Global Footprint Network data give Japan an ecological footprint of about 4.4 global hectares (gha) per person and a biocapacity of 0.6 gha per person. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Calculate (a) the ecological balance per person and (b) how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average resident.
items.answer: (a) -3.8 gha per person (ecological deficit) (b) 4.4 / 1.6 ≈ 2.8 Earths
items.markingKey: (a) M1 biocapacity − footprint, A1 -3.8 gha and correct label. (b) M1 A1 2.8 Earths.

items.stem: Estimates for Mexico give a crude birth rate (CBR) of 14.0 per 1,000 and a crude death rate (CDR) of 7.6 per 1,000. Calculate (i) the rate of natural increase as a percentage and (ii) the doubling time, using the rule of 70.
Outline one way in which Costa Rica's Payment for Environmental Services programme shows national-scale resource stewardship.
items.answer: Landowners have been paid to conserve or restore forest since 1997, and forest cover rose to over 50%. Economic incentives can reverse deforestation.
items.markingKey: Context (Landowners have been paid to conserve or restore forest since 1997, and forest cover rose to over 50%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Economic incentives can reverse deforestation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to national-scale resource stewardship.

items.stem: Briefly describe the EU Circular Economy Action Plan (2020) and explain what it reveals about regional-scale stewardship policy.
items.answer: Targets include 65% recycling of municipal waste by 2035 and a "right to repair". Legislation sets targets and responsibilities that change producer and consumer behaviour.
items.markingKey: Context (Targets include 65% recycling of municipal waste by 2035 and a "right to repair".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Legislation sets targets and responsibilities that change producer and consumer behaviour. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to regional-scale stewardship policy.

items.stem: Kenya: ecological footprint ≈ 1.0 gha/person; biocapacity ≈ 0.5 gha/person. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Calculate (a) the ecological balance per person and (b) how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average resident.
